1.pericope_label: But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them — and many shall follow their pernicious ways, by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of

schools.summary: Begin with the offense to weak consciences: they are grievously shaken when false teachers arise who corrupt or mutilate the doctrine of faith, and so the apostle removes the offense out of the way by showing that God has always tried and proved his Church by this temptation, that novelty might not disturb their hearts. The condition of the Church under the gospel will not differ from what it was under the law; false prophets disturbed the ancient Church, and the same must be expected by us. Say this expressly, because many imagined that the Church would enjoy tranquillity under the reign of Christ, the prophets having promised that at his coming there would be real peace and the full restoration of all things, so that they thought the Church would be no more exposed to contests. Let us remember that the Spirit has once for all declared that the Church shall never be free from this intestine evil, and that the trial of our faith is to be similar to that of the fathers, and for the same reason, that in this way it may be made evident whether we really love God. Observe that no one time in particular is named, but that all ages are included, so the truth is to be applied to our own time. Note also that the apostle does not paint each sect in its own colours but particularly refers to profane men who manifested contempt towards God, selecting the one kind from whom the greater danger arose. On the privy bringing in, point out the craftiness of Satan and of all who militate under his banner, that they would creep in by oblique turnings, as through burrows under ground, under the colour of true doctrine and by little and little, so that the people would not discern their real nature; the more watchful, then, ought the godly to be. On the heresies, say that the word has always and not without reason been deemed infamous and hateful by the children of God, since the bond of holy unity is the simple truth, and as soon as we depart from that nothing remains but dreadful discord. On the denial, say that though Christ may be denied in various ways, the reference here is to turning the grace of God into lasciviousness, for Christ redeemed us that he might have a people separated from all the pollutions of the world and devoted to holiness; they who throw off the bridle and give themselves up to licentiousness are not unjustly said to deny the Christ by whom they have been redeemed. On the many followers, admit that it is no slight offense to the weak to see false doctrines received by the common consent of the world, since hardly one in ten of those who have once professed Christ retains the purity of faith to the end. On the variant, report that some copies read lasciviousness and others perdition, that very few have perdition and very many lasciviousness with the versions, and follow the reading mostly approved. And explain the evil speaking thus: as religion is adorned when men are taught to fear God and maintain uprightness of life, so when the reins are let loose the name and doctrine of Christ are exposed to the reproaches of the ungodly — not that these teachers themselves assail the faith with calumnies, but that they give enemies occasion to assail it. Elsewhere, on the people among whom the false prophets arose, name Jeremiah’s time and Ezekiel’s, and Ahab’s four hundred who called themselves prophets of the Lord and among whom a lying spirit went forth. And on the many followers, say that the road both of error and wickedness is a broad one in which many walk, and that a multitude is no proof of the truth of a church nor to be followed.

Bring out the contrast in the form of the sentence: the clause secondary in meaning has been made primary in form, so that the sense is, there shall be false teachers among you as there were false prophets among the Jews. Note that the word for false teachers occurs here only, that it is probably analogous to false witnesses and so means those who teach what is false rather than those pretending to be teachers, and that false prophets carries both meanings. Note that the writer pictures these men in the future here, as already present later in the chapter, and in the past a few verses further on. Take the word rendered heresies as simply a choosing, a school, a sect, used of the Sadducees and of the Pharisees and of Christians as one apostle himself admitted; then argue that neither sect nor heresy gives the true meaning in the New Testament, where it points rather to divisions than doctrines and always to parties inside the Church, not to sects that have separated from it — damnable heresies comes from the Geneva version, altogether a change for the worse, where the older versions have sects of perdition. Add the count: the Greek word for destruction occurs six times in this short letter and is rendered by our translators in no less than five different ways. On the denial, note that the word for Master is the old word for an absolute owner, without the evil sense of our despot, and that the participle for bought carries the same idea as the word for ransom in the first epistle — so these heretics were at any rate professing Christians. Say that the text is conclusive against Calvinistic doctrines of partial redemption, since the apostle declares that these impious false teachers were redeemed. Observe that the phrase is remarkable as coming from one who himself denied his Master, and ask whether a forger would have ventured to make him write thus; and note in passing that denying was the very thing this apostle did, even after his Lord’s warning. Collect the external evidence as you go: a mid-second-century apologist writing to a Jew has just as there were false prophets contemporaneous with your holy prophets, so are there now many false teachers amongst us; a homily doubtfully attributed to a Roman writer quotes the verse outright; and the phrase the way of truth occurs in an Alexandrian father, the only near approach to anything in this letter in all his surviving writings, which is strong evidence that he did not know it, especially as he refers often to the first epistle and sometimes quotes it by name. On the second verse, prefer the marginal reading, lascivious or wanton ways, the plural of the word rendered wantonness later in the chapter; note that a large number of manuscripts and versions support it and that three modern editors have adopted it, and that this agrees with the account given of these teachers elsewhere in the chapter. Then observe that men who deny the essential doctrines of the gospel have very frequently been licentious in their own conduct and have inculcated opinions tending to licentiousness, since men corrupt at heart seek the sanction of religion for their corruptions — or else warn that while the connection between false doctrine and licentiousness was often real, and is so still in some cases, it was as often asserted and believed without foundation, impurity being the common charge to bring against those of a different creed, whether between heathen and Christian or between different divisions of Christians. Take the ones by reason of whom the way is blasphemed to be the many led astray rather than the original seducers, and note that the way of truth stands in the Greek Old Testament for the right road, which is what is meant here.

Set the chapter against the end of the last: there mention was made of holy men of God used as the amanuenses of the Holy Ghost in writing the sacred oracles, but here we are told they had even then false prophets in the church as well as true. In all ages of the church and under all dispensations, when God sends true prophets the devil sends some to seduce and deceive — false prophets under the Old Testament, and false Christs, false apostles and seducing teachers in the New. Observe of these: that their business is to bring in destructive errors, even damnable heresies, as the business of teachers sent of God is to show the way of truth; that there are damnable heresies as well as damnable practices, and false teachers are industrious to spread pernicious errors; that damnable heresies are commonly brought in privily, under the cloak and colour of truth; that those who introduce them deny the Lord that bought them, refusing to hear and learn of the great teacher sent from God, though he is the only Saviour and Redeemer of men, who paid a price sufficient to redeem as many worlds of sinners as there are sinners in the world; and that those who bring in errors destructive to others bring swift and therefore sure destruction on themselves, for self-destroyers are soon destroyed. Then on the consequence to others: corrupt leaders seldom fail of many to follow them, for though the way of error is a pernicious way many are ready to walk in it — men drink in iniquity like water and are pleased to live in error, the prophets prophesy falsely and the people love to have it so. And the spreading of error will bring up an evil report on the way of truth, that is, the way of salvation by Jesus Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life; the Christian religion is from the God of truth as its author, leads to the enjoyment of the true God as its end, and works truth in the inward part as its means, and yet is traduced and blasphemed by those who advance destructive errors. Let us not be offended at any of this in our own day, but take care that we give no occasion to the enemy to blaspheme the holy name whereby we are called.

Say that there were not only holy men among the Jews who prophesied by divine inspiration but also false prophets whose prophecies were from their own imagination; and add the finer point, that those who spake even the truth when God had not sent them, and those truly sent who corrupted or softened their message, were alike false prophets. On the sects, say that at a very early period many heresies sprang up, chiefly those of the Ebionites, Cerinthians, Nicolaitans, Menandrians and Gnostics, of whom many strange things have been spoken by the primitive fathers and of whose opinions it is difficult to form any satisfactory view — they were no doubt bad enough, and their opponents in general have doubtless made them worse; by what name those the apostle speaks of were called we cannot tell. Render the phrase heresies of destruction, such as if followed would lead a man to perdition, and say it would be better to translate destructive heresies than damnable; note that the verb means they will bring them in privately, cunningly, without making much noise and as covertly as possible. On the denial, allow that it is not certain whether God the Father is intended, since God is said to have purchased Israel, or our Lord Jesus Christ, who bought them with his blood; but conclude that it seems more natural to understand it of Christ, and draw two inferences — that none can be saved but by him, and that through their own wickedness some may perish for whom he died. Elsewhere put it flatly: yet these very men perish everlastingly, therefore Christ bought even them that perish. On the heresies say they are divisions, and leave open whether they are the effect of denying the Lord or its cause. On the second verse, give the manuscript evidence at length for lasciviousnesses against destructions — upwards of sixty manuscripts, mostly the most ancient and correct, with both Syriac versions, all the Arabic, the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonic and Latin, and several Greek fathers — and say the word points out what the nature of the heresies was, a sort of Antinomianism in which the lusts of the flesh were pampered and indulged. And press the reproach home: these were persons who professed Christianity, and because they were called Christians and followed such practices the Christian religion was blasphemed; had they called themselves by any name but Christ’s, his religion would not have suffered. Add that the way of truth is evil spoken of by those who blend all false and true Christians together.

debates: Whether the clause about being bought disproves a limited redemption.
Whether the received text reads pernicious ways or lascivious ways.
Whether damnable heresies renders a word that means doctrines or divisions.
Whether the Lord who bought them is the Father or the Son.
Whether the charge of licentiousness against heretics is generally credible.
outliers: Ellicott calls the verse conclusive against Calvinistic partial redemption; Calvin answers by reading the denial as practical, not doctrinal.
Gill’s note stops mid-sentence before reaching the disputed clause, so the reformed side loses its fullest voice on it.
Clarke warns that the heretics’ opponents have doubtless made them worse than they were.
Ellicott traces damnable heresies to the Geneva version and calls it a change for the worse.
Ellicott counts one Greek word rendered five different ways in a single short letter.
Barnes finds the link between false doctrine and licentiousness remarkable; Ellicott warns it was as often a slander as a fact.
Ellicott runs an attestation argument through his notes, using a father’s silence as evidence he did not know the epistle.

3.pericope_label: And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you, whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not — for if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell — and spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness

schools.summary: Explain the covetousness as motive: the religious principle is the strongest implanted in the human bosom, and men who can obtain a livelihood in no other way, or who are too unprincipled or indolent to labour for an honest living, often turn public teachers of religion and adopt the kind of doctrines likeliest to give them power over the purses of others — true religion does require its friends to devote all they have to the service of God, but it is very easy to pervert that requirement to the teacher’s own aggrandisement. Or read the preposition as in covetousness, the atmosphere in which they live, and compare the man who offered the apostle money and was doubtless accustomed to take it for his own teaching; say these teachers, like the Greek sophists, taught for money, and that a bombastic mysticism promising to reveal secrets about the unseen world and the future was a very lucrative profession in the last days of paganism which passed over into Christianity as an element in various heresies. Take the word for merchandise from the verb meaning to travel as a merchant on business, and so to deal in, to make merchandise of — treating men not as rational beings but as a bale of goods. Render the feigned words as forged words, from a verbal adjective of the verb to mould as from clay, occurring here only; and note that the doctrines were not maintained by solid argument but by plausible reasoning made up for the occasion. On the sentence, say the word means the verdict and not the process, that the adverb for of old is late and common, that the verb rendered lingereth means literally is not idle, and that the word for slumbering occurs elsewhere only in the parable of the virgins; note also that the noun for destruction has now stood three times in three verses, and that the destruction involved in the judgment is awake and on its way to overtake them. On the angels, note the condition has no expressed apodosis here, and either say that the sentence has no proper conclusion, the third instance being so prolonged by the addition about Lot that the writer in his eagerness lost the thread of the construction, or find the answer implied in the ninth verse. Observe that the three instances stand here in chronological order where the parallel epistle has them otherwise. Then press the question what sin is meant: not the fall of the angels that preceded human history, of which there is no record in the Old Testament and which affords no close analogy to the conduct of these teachers, but the sin of the sons of God in Genesis, or more probably the frequent statements in the Book of Enoch that certain angels sinned by intercourse with women — and note that these false teachers not improbably used that book in their own corrupt teaching, so that the argument is turned against them from their own authority. Add that Tartarus occurs in Enoch as the place of punishment of the fallen angels, while Gehenna is for apostate Jews; that the verb for casting down is formed from that name and is found here alone; and that the manuscripts vary between the word for chains and the word for pits, the latter being right. On the flood, take Noah the eighth by the common Greek idiom for Noah and seven others, the point being that the punishment must have been signal indeed if only eight escaped out of a whole world; dismiss as gratuitous the suggestion that eight is a mystical number, and as utterly pointless the notion that eighth means eighth from Enos, there being neither mention of Enos nor the faintest allusion to him; and judge that taking the numeral with preacher rather than with Noah is hardly correct. Note the coincidence with the first epistle, where spirits in prison are mentioned immediately before, just as here the angels in caves of darkness.

Say the apostle endeavours by all means to render the faithful displeased with ungodly teachers, that they may resist them more resolutely; it is an especially odious thing that we should be exposed to sale like vile slaves, and this is done when anyone seduces us from the redemption of Christ. On the feigned words, allow two senses: either words not conveying the speaker’s real sentiments but adopted to allure others, as with those who pretend great zeal for truth and great love for souls when their object is to gain adherents for filthy lucre; or else invented narratives and fables, such as the visions of angels and the miracles performed at the sepulchres of departed saints, which false teachers in the early ages and monks in later times fabricated to draw money from the people — and similar are the devices of superstitious men greedy of gain in every age. Unless a man is mad enough to sell the salvation of his soul, let him close up every avenue that may lead to their wicked inventions. Repeat that their destruction is not delayed, in order to frighten the good from their society, since everyone who connects himself with them must perish with them. Then prove that the ungodly cannot escape God’s vengeance by three remarkable examples of judgment: that he spared not even angels, that he once destroyed the whole world by a deluge, and that he reduced Sodom to ashes. Take as granted what ought never to be doubted, that God is judge of the whole world; it follows that the punishment he formerly inflicted on the wicked he will now inflict on the like characters, for he can never be unlike himself, nor does he show respect of persons so as to forgive in one the wickedness he punished in another. On the broken construction, note that some supply at the end of the seventh verse he will not spare thee, but there is no need of this, since the corresponding clause is in the ninth verse, where the deliverance of the just is first mentioned and then the reservation of the unjust for judgment — a sort of arrangement common in Scripture. On the flood, say God formed as it were a new world after drowning the human race, and argue from the greater to the less: how shall the wicked escape the deluge of divine wrath, since the whole world was once destroyed by it? By saying that eight only were saved he intimates that a multitude is no shield against God, but that as many as sin shall be punished, be they few or many. On the title given to Noah, report that some understand him to be the preacher of the righteousness of God, but think rather that he is so called because he laboured to restore a degenerated world to a sound mind, not only by teaching and godly exhortations but by his anxious toil in building the ark for the term of a hundred and twenty years. Elsewhere note that covetousness generally prevails among false teachers, who have no end in view but themselves, either to gain popular applause and vain glory or to amass riches after an insatiable desire; that by the angels are meant the devil and his angels, spirits created good, once among the morning stars and sons of God, whose first sin is generally thought to have been pride, affecting a likeness to God, since this was what man was tempted to by them; and that the old world means the ancient inhabitants before the flood, as distinguished from the present world formed anew out of what the deluge destroyed.

Warn against the common mistake: men are apt to think that a reprieve is the forerunner of a pardon, and that if judgment be not speedily executed it will certainly be reversed; but however successful and prosperous false teachers may be for a time, their judgment lingereth not, God having determined long ago how he will deal with them. Such unbelievers, who endeavour to turn others from the faith, are condemned already, and the wrath of God abideth on them; the righteous Judge will speedily take vengeance, the day of their calamity is at hand. Then set out the examples. See how God dealt with the angels who sinned, and observe: that no excellency will exempt a sinner from punishment, since if angels, who excel us vastly in strength and knowledge, violate the law of God, the sentence shall be executed on them without mercy or mitigation, for God did not spare them; that by how much the more excellent the offender, by so much the more severe the punishment, these angels being immediately punished with no sparing for a few days and no favour shown; that sin debases and degrades those who commit it, the angels of heaven being cast down from the height of their excellency and divested of all their glory upon their disobedience, so that whoever sins against God does manifest hurt to himself; and that those who rebel against the God of heaven shall all be sent down to hell, there being no place nor state between the height of glory and the depth of misery in which they may rest — if creatures sin in heaven, they must suffer in hell.

On the covetousness, say they sought money to spend upon their lusts, and take the feigned words as counterfeit tales, false narrations of pretended facts, lying miracles and fabulous legends; then quote the judgment of another writer, that in this single sentence there is a clear prediction of the iniquitous practices of those great merchants of souls, the Romish clergy, who have rated all crimes, even the most atrocious, at a fixed price, so that if their doctrine be true whoever pays the price may commit the crime without hazarding his salvation — and add that it was this abominable doctrine which showed some then in that Church the absolute necessity of a reformation. Say that from the beginning God has condemned sin and inflicted suitable punishments, so the condemnation denounced against these slumbers not: it is alert, it is on its way, it is hurrying on and must soon overtake them; all sinners are adjudged to destruction, and God’s punishing some proves he will punish the rest. On the angels, say they were originally placed in a state of probation, since some fell and some stood; how long that probation was to last, what the test of their fidelity was, what their sin was, when and how they fell, we do not know. The tradition of their fall is in all countries and in all religions, but the accounts given are various and contradictory, and no wonder, for we have no direct revelation on the subject — they kept not their first estate, and they sinned, is the sum of what we know, and here curiosity and conjecture are useless. Call chains of darkness a highly poetic expression: darkness binds them on all hands, and is so dense and strong that it cannot be broken through, so they can neither deliver themselves nor be delivered by others — though those chains do not hinder their often walking up and down seeking whom they may devour. Note that the word Tartarus is found nowhere else in the New Testament nor in the Greek Old Testament, so that recourse must be had to the Greek writers for its meaning, and have that recourse at length. On the flood, give the arithmetic: eight persons were saved in the ark, three sons and their three wives, Noah’s wife, and Noah himself the eighth; and defend the form of expression by parallels from the Greek historians, where a man called the third or the tenth means himself and two or nine others. Call the drowned a whole race without God, without any pure worship or rational religion, whose numbers stood them in no stead.

debates: Whether the sentence beginning with if has lost its conclusion.
What sin the angels committed.
Whether Noah the eighth means Noah and seven others or the eighth preacher.
Whether the feigned words are insincere speech or invented tales.
Whether the manuscripts read chains of darkness or pits of darkness.
outliers: Ellicott says the writer lost the thread of his own sentence; Calvin says nothing is missing and points to the ninth verse.
Ellicott rejects the primeval fall of the angels and reads the verse from the Book of Enoch, suggesting the false teachers had used that book themselves.
Robertson independently notes that Enoch assigns Tartarus to fallen angels and Gehenna to apostate Jews.
Clarke and the editorial matter printed with Calvin both apply the verse to the medieval Roman clergy, from opposite sides of the Reformation.
Clarke observes that the tradition of a fall of angels is universal but that the accounts contradict each other, so conjecture is useless.
Ellicott dismisses two proposed readings of the number eight as gratuitous and pointless.
Calvin explains preacher of righteousness by the hundred and twenty years of building rather than by anything Noah said.

6.pericope_label: And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly — and delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked — for that righteous man dwelling among them vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds

schools.summary: Note that the word rendered turning into ashes occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, being formed from the noun for ashes and meaning to reduce to ashes and so to destroy, a late word used by one historian of an eruption of Vesuvius. Say that by the fact of their overthrow God showed he disapproved their conduct, their calamity coming expressly on account of their enormous sins, as it frequently happens now that the judgments which come upon the licentious are as plain a proof of divine disapprobation; and that the punishment of one wicked man or people always becomes a warning to all others. Observe that the very word used for overthrow is the word the Greek Old Testament uses of the overthrow of these cities, that it occurs once elsewhere in the New Testament, and that it may be read as condemned them to an overthrow, like condemn to death; note also that some editors reject the word here on the authority of certain manuscripts and a version. On Lot, prefer righteous to just, since it is the same adjective which occurs twice more in the next verse; and take the difficulty head on — the epithet seems at first sight at variance with his willingness to remain, for the sake of worldly advantages, in the midst of such wickedness, but righteous is a relative term, and he must be looked at in comparison both with the defective morality of the age and with the licentiousness of those he is contrasted with. Add that in the midst of the corruption he preserved the brighter features of his purer nomad life, especially the chivalrous hospitality to which the epistle to the Hebrews seems to point as a model; add the rescue of him and his family, taken with the declaration that ten righteous people would have saved the whole city, his ready belief and obedience when told to leave all, and the sparing of Zoar at his intercession — and the epithet is by no means without warrant. On the construction of the next verse, report the Latin rendering, that in seeing and hearing he was just, which many expositors have supposed correct, but prefer the natural and common explanation, that being compelled while living among them to see and hear what was going on, his soul was constantly troubled; note the effect on Lot is not mentioned in Genesis, and that whether the statement rests on tradition or on inspiration cannot be determined. Take the two nouns as instrumental, by sight and by hearing, note the idiom day in day out, and observe that the verb for vexing is in a tense of continued action, an old word used of testing metals and then of tormenting. Then turn the repetitions to account: this Epistle repeats words — destruction three times in three verses, righteous three times here, and other instances later — and such repetition has been stigmatised as poverty of language; but it is perfectly natural in a man writing under strong emotion, who does not stop to pick his words but uses the same one over again if it says what he means, and still more natural in one writing a foreign language. It is not like the laboured effort of a writer endeavouring to personate him, and the fact that such repetitions are frequent in this letter but not in the first is fully explained by the circumstances and may be regarded as a mark of genuineness. Note finally that here, as with the Flood, the destruction of the guilty suggests the preservation of the innocent, that this brighter side is wanting in the parallel epistle, and ask whether it is fanciful to think these lights in a dark picture characteristic of one who had himself denied the Master who bought him and had yet been preserved like Noah and rescued like Lot.

Say of Sodom that this was so memorable an example of divine vengeance that when Scripture speaks of the universal destruction of the ungodly it commonly alludes to this as the type; others might truly be so described, but something singular is pointed out here, because it was the chief and a lively image, and because the Lord designed that his wrath against the ungodly should be made known to all ages — as when he redeemed his people from Egypt he set forth by that one favour the perpetual safety of his Church. On the construction of the eighth verse, report the common explanation, that Lot was just in his eyes and ears because all his senses abhorred the crimes of Sodom, but take another view: that when the just man lived among the Sodomites he tormented his soul by seeing and hearing, since we know he was constrained to see and hear many things which greatly vexed his mind. The purport is that though the holy man was surrounded with every kind of monstrous wickedness he never turned aside from his upright course; but more than that is expressed, namely that just Lot underwent voluntary sorrows. As it is right that all the godly should feel no small grief when they see the world rushing into every kind of evil, so the more necessary is it that they should groan for their own sins; and this was expressly mentioned lest, when impiety everywhere prevails, we should be captivated and inebriated by the allurements of vices and perish together with others, and that we might prefer this grief, blessed by the Lord, to all the pleasures of the world. Elsewhere, describe the cities as delightfully situated, as the garden of God, destroyed after they had received a signal mercy in being rescued from the kings who carried them captive, and though Abraham interceded for them and righteous Lot dwelt among them; collect what the Greek and Jewish writers call them and whether the name stands in the singular or the plural. And on Lot, say he was a just man, justified by the righteousness of Christ imputed to him, having the new man formed in him, living soberly and righteously though not without sin, for there is not a just man that lives and sinneth not — then set down honestly what the Jewish writers say against him, that they call him a wicked man, a perfect wicked man, as wicked as the inhabitants of Sodom, that because they abounded in sin he chose to dwell among them, that all the time he was with Abraham God did not commune with Abraham on his account, and that they call him the evil imagination and the old serpent; and note that one Jewish writer of another school speaks better of him.

Lay down the rule: when God sends destruction on the ungodly he commands deliverance for the righteous, and if he rain fire and brimstone on the wicked he will cover the head of the just, who shall be hid in the day of his anger — of which the preserving of Lot is the instance. Observe the character given of him: he is called a just man, and this he was as to the generally prevailing bent of his heart and the main of his conversation, for God does not account men just or unjust from one single act but from their general course of life; and here is a just man in the midst of a most corrupt and profligate generation universally gone off from all good, who does not follow the multitude to do evil but in a city of injustice walks uprightly. Observe next the impression the sins of others made upon him: though the sinner takes pleasure in his wickedness, it is a grief and vexation to the soul of the righteous, and in bad company we cannot escape either guilt or grief — let the sins of others be a trouble to us, otherwise it will not be possible for us to keep ourselves pure. And observe the duration of the grief: it was from day to day, being accustomed to hear and see their wickedness did not reconcile him to it nor abate the horror it occasioned. From this instance we are taught to argue that God knows how to deliver his people and to punish his enemies.

Refer the reader to the history in Genesis for the sin and the punishment of the cities, and comment chiefly on words. Distinguish the three Greek nouns used for an example — the first perhaps meaning an example to be shunned, the second an example to be followed, the third a simple exhibition — and then admit that these differences are not always observed. Render the seventh verse as being exceedingly pained with the unclean conduct of those lawless persons. On the eighth, do the arithmetic: Lot, after his departure from Abraham, lived at Sodom about twenty years, and as he had a righteous soul he must have been tormented with the abominations of that people from day to day. And note that the verb rendered tormented in the second verse is not less emphatic than the participle rendered grievously pained in the first, which shows what such a man must have felt in dwelling so long among a people so abandoned.

debates: Whether the epithet righteous can properly be applied to Lot.
Whether the eighth verse says Lot was just in seeing and hearing, or that he was tormented by them.
Whether the repetitions of a single word in this letter tell against its authorship.
Whether the word rendered overthrow belongs in the text at all.
What the example of Sodom was meant to prove.
outliers: Gill records the Jewish tradition that Lot was as wicked as the Sodomites, and rejects it.
Ellicott builds a five-point defence of Lot from Genesis and Hebrews.
Barnes reports that the Latin version construes the eighth verse in a way many expositors have followed and he does not.
Ellicott turns a stylistic complaint against the epistle into an argument for its genuineness.
Ellicott notes that the deliverance of the righteous, present here, is absent from the parallel epistle, and reads it as personal.
Robertson finds the verb for turning to ashes used elsewhere only of an eruption of Vesuvius.
Clarke draws a three-way distinction between Greek words for example and then withdraws it.

9.pericope_label: The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished — but chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government: presumptuous are they, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities

schools.summary: Say this is the main sentence to which the conditional clauses have been leading, or the actual apodosis of the long protasis begun at the angels; but note also that the construction is disjointed, owing to the eagerness of the writer, that the main clause does not fit on to the introductory clauses very smoothly, and that it is itself interrupted by the insertion about delivering the godly, when what the writer specially wishes to prove is that the Lord knows how to reserve the ungodly for the day of judgment under punishment. Correct the tense: the participle is present, not future, so read not to be punished but being punished, or under punishment — they are already suffering while waiting for their final doom — and note that the error in our version is parallel to the one which gives such as should be saved instead of those who were being saved; the present tense emphasises the continuity of the punishment. On the deliverance, say the cases cited show that God is able to deliver his people when tempted and understands the best way to do it: he sees a way when we cannot, though often a way we should not have thought of, and he can send an angel to take his tempted people by the hand, destroy the power of the tempter, raise up earthly friends, or deliver them for ever by their removal to heaven; and as the case of the angels shows, he can keep wicked men as if under bonds, reserved for their final trial, so that though they seem to go at large they are under his control. Note that the same double moral, that God will save the righteous and punish the ungodly, is drawn from the same instance by an early Roman writer. On the tenth verse, note the phrase after the flesh is a Hebraism, that it is less definite here than in the parallel epistle, where there is something about the flesh being other than is allowed, so that the parallel applies to the men of the cities of the plain in particular and this to sensual persons generally; render the next words the lust of pollution, that is, the lust which causes pollution, and note that the exact word occurs nowhere else. Then complain of the version: it is minutely perverse here, rendering by government and by dominion one and the same Greek word in the two places, while rendering by despise two words that differ. Say a fresh verse should begin at presumptuous, the construction being entirely changed and a fresh start made, since from the unjust to government the reference is to ungodly and sensual people in general and here we return to the false teachers in particular; render the word audacious rather than presumptuous, and note it is found here only, as is the noun for daring men, and that self-willed means self-pleasing or arrogant. And on the dignities, take the harder line: the exact meaning is not clear either here or in the parallel, but the context in both places seems to show that spiritual powers alone are intended, and that earthly powers, whether civil or ecclesiastical, are not included, much less exclusively indicated — these men deny the existence of, or irreverently speak slightingly of, those spiritual agencies by means of which God conducts the government of the world. Or say more cautiously that perhaps these dignities are angels. Elsewhere, if you take them for men of exalted rank, say the offenders regard all government in the state, the church and the family as an evil, that they are advocates for unbridled freedom of all sorts, declaimers on liberty and on the evils of oppression, defenders of what they regard as the rights of injured man, and yet secretly themselves lusting for the exercise of the very power they would deny to others; no topic of declamation would be more popular, for if they could remove all respect for the just restraints of law the way would be open to set up a dominion over the minds of others, and men of this description commonly become impatient of the government of God himself.

Name the two things that offend the weak: that when the faithful anxiously seek aid they are not immediately helped, but are suffered sometimes to pine away through daily weariness; and that the wicked grow wanton with impunity while God is silent, as though he connived at their evil deeds. Remove both offences by testifying that the Lord knows when it is expedient to deliver the godly from temptation, and so remind us that this office is to be left to him, that we are to endure temptations and not faint when he defers his vengeance. This consolation is very necessary, for the thought is apt to creep in: if the Lord would have his own to be safe, why does he not gather them all into some corner of the earth, that they may mutually stimulate one another to holiness? why does he mingle them with the wicked by whom they may be defiled? But when God claims to himself the office of helping and protecting his own, we gather courage to fight more strenuously. The law prescribed to all the godly is that they are to be proved by various temptations, but they are to entertain good hope of success, because they are never to be deprived of his aid; and God so regulates his judgments as to bear with the wicked for a time, but not to leave them unpunished, which corrects our haste. Then come to particulars, since he had to do with men of desperate wickedness: to walk after the flesh is to be given up to the flesh like brute animals, who are not led by reason and judgment but have the natural desire of their flesh as their chief guide; and by the lust of uncleanness understand filthy and unbridled gratifications, when men, having cast away every virtuous feeling and shaken off shame, are carried away into every uncleanness. This is the first mark by which he brands them. Then point out the fountain of their contempt of government, that they were self-pleasing, whose ruling principle was to gratify themselves without regarding God’s will or the good of others, whose god was self — and such selfish men are commonly haughty, arrogant and refractory. And say that it is a monstrous arrogance to regard as nothing the glory which shines forth in dignities appointed by God; there is no doubt that these words refer to the imperial and magisterial power, for though no lawful station in life is unworthy of respect, the magisterial office excels every other. Elsewhere take the temptations out of which the godly are delivered to be not the temptations of Satan to sin or despondency but afflictions and tribulations, such as Noah and Lot were exposed to, so called because they try the graces and particularly the faith and patience of the godly; and take walking after the flesh to mean not merely following the dictates of corrupt nature, as all men do in a state of unregeneracy, but going after strange flesh.

Return now to the seducers, and give an account of their character and conduct, which abundantly justifies the righteous Judge in reserving them in an especial manner for the most severe and heavy doom, as Cain was taken under a special protection that he might be kept for uncommon vengeance. Why will God deal thus with these false teachers? Because they walk after the flesh: they follow the devices and desires of their own hearts, give themselves up to the conduct of their own fleshly mind, refuse to make their reason stoop to divine revelation and to bring every thought to the obedience of Christ, and act directly contrary to God’s righteous precepts. Evil opinions are often accompanied with evil practices, and those who are for propagating error are for improving in wickedness: they will not sit down contented in the measure of iniquity to which they have attained, nor is it enough for them to stand up and defend the wickedness they have already committed, but they go on in their sinful course and increase unto more ungodliness. They also pour contempt on those whom God has set in authority over them and requires them to honour, and so despise the ordinance of God; and we need not wonder at it, for they are bold and daring, obstinate and refractory, and will not only cherish contempt in their hearts but with their tongues will utter slanderous and reproachful words of those set over them.

Draw the doctrine from the deliverance of Lot: God knows as well to save as to destroy, and his goodness led him as forcibly to save righteous Lot as his justice did to destroy the rebellious; the design of the examples is to show the readers that although God would destroy the false teachers, he would powerfully save his faithful servants from their contagion and from their destruction. Then set down carefully what is and is not promised: first, that the godly man is not to be preserved from temptation; second, that he will be preserved in temptation; third, that he will be delivered out of it. Say plainly that it appears from these instances that the Lord knoweth, that is, hath both wisdom and power and will, to deliver the godly out of all temptations and to punish the ungodly. On the tenth verse, say God will in the most signal manner punish those who addict themselves to the practices named, and name them; and on despising government, say they brave the power and authority of the civil magistrate, practising their abominations so as to keep out of the reach of the letter of the law, that they blaspheme civil government, abhor the restraints laid on men by the laws, and would wish all governments destroyed that they might live as they list. Render the next words as bold and daring, headstrong, regardless of fear; and self-willed as self-sufficient, presuming on themselves, following their own opinions, which no authority can induce them to relinquish. Say those in general despise governments and speak evil of dignities who wish to be under no control, that they may act as freebooters in the community. Elsewhere gloss the terms as briefly as possible: government is the authority of their governors, and dignities are persons in authority.

debates: Whether the dignities railed at are civil magistrates or spiritual powers.
Whether the unjust are reserved to be punished or are already under punishment.
Where the long conditional sentence finds its main clause.
What the temptations are out of which the godly are delivered.
Whether a new verse ought to begin in the middle of the tenth.
outliers: Ellicott and Robertson read the dignities as spiritual powers; Calvin, Barnes, Clarke and Wesley read them as civil authority.
Ellicott corrects a future to a present participle and makes the ungodly already under punishment.
Ellicott calls the English version minutely perverse for rendering one Greek word two ways and two Greek words one way.
Clarke reduces the promise to a three-part rule that denies exemption from temptation.
Calvin frames the passage as the answer to an objection he states in full before answering it.
Barnes reads the contempt of government as a description of political radicalism of his own day.
Gill takes walking after the flesh to mean strange flesh, narrowing what the others leave general.

11.pericope_label: Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord — but these, as natural brute beasts, made to be taken and destroyed, speak evil of the things that they understand not — and shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time

schools.summary: Say the object of the reference to angels is to show that even when manifesting the greatest zeal in a righteous cause, and even when opposing others, they did not make use of reproachful terms or of harsh and violent language; admit that it is not known precisely what is alluded to nor on what the statement rests, but note the strong resemblance to the parallel epistle and the probability that both refer to the same Jewish tradition of the archangel contending with the devil about the body of Moses, so that though the plural is used the single case was probably in view. Then use these verses to weigh which epistle came first. The eleventh, if it refers to the same incident, seems at first sight to tell somewhat in favour of the other’s priority, since only by comparison with it does this become intelligible, the inference being that this is an abbreviation rather than that an amplification. But such an inference is at best only probable: the writer might count on his readers understanding at once an allusion to a well-known tradition, while the other thought it best to point it out more plainly; or the contest alluded to may be not that over the body of Moses but that between Satan and the angel of the Lord about the high priest in Zechariah; or it may refer to no contest with Satan at all, but merely to angels not denouncing these false teachers before God but leaving them to His judgment. If either of the last two is correct, the argument for the other epistle’s priority falls to the ground; and if the first is right, the argument really favours this one, for a writer who had the other before him and wished to use the illustration would hardly deface it so. The twelfth verse, on the other hand, tells strongly in favour of this epistle’s priority: the literary form of the parallel is so very superior, its antithesis between abusing what they cannot know and misusing what they cannot help knowing so telling and so easily remembered, that a writer willing to adopt so much would hardly have failed to adopt that too, whereas there is nothing improbable in a writer who knew this verse improving on it. On the beasts themselves, omit the word natural as an epithet and take it adverbially — born naturally for capture and destruction — the force being that these animals cannot help themselves, since it is their nature to rush after what will prove their ruin, whereas the false teachers voluntarily seek their own destruction against nature. Note that the words for destruction and corruption here are one and the same in the Greek, another of the repetitions characteristic of this letter, and observe the rhetorical Hebraism in shall in their destroying surely be destroyed. Say that a man who sinks himself to the level of brutes must expect to be treated like brutes, since man, though he has passions resembling those of the brute creation, is endowed with a higher nature designed to control them. On the thirteenth verse, begin a fresh sentence and modify the rendering: to riot is too strong, the word meaning delicate fare, dainty living, luxury; and since dainty fare in the day time has little point, read perhaps for the day, without thought for the morrow, counting the luxury of the moment a pleasure — the doctrine of the Cyrenaics and the instinct of the brute beasts. Note that the following participle is a compound of the same word, so luxuriating, and that the words for spots and blemishes correspond exactly to the words rendered without blemish and without spot in the first epistle. On the last variant, report that several versions and a few manuscripts read love-feasts for deceivings, the two words differing by little in Greek, and judge the common reading undoubtedly correct; or set the manuscripts of each side against each other and note that if love-feasts is genuine here, this and the parallel are the only instances of that use of the word in the New Testament.

Show their rash arrogance, that they dared assume more liberty than even angels. But meet the objection: it seems strange to say that angels do not bring a railing accusation against magistrates, for why should they be adverse to that sacred order whose author they know to be God, or oppose rulers whom they know to exercise the same ministry with themselves? This reasoning has made some think that the devils are meant, but they do not thus escape the difficulty, for how could Satan be so moderate as to spare men, since he is the author of every blasphemy against God? And their opinion is refuted by the parallel epistle. When we consider the circumstances of the time, what is said applies very suitably to holy angels: all the magistrates were then ungodly and bloody enemies to the gospel, and must therefore have been hateful to angels, the guardians of the Church; yet men deserving hatred and execration were not condemned by them, in order that they might show respect to a power divinely appointed — and while such moderation is shown by angels, these men fearlessly give vent to unbridled blasphemies. Then condemn the loose manners and the obscene wickedness of their whole life, and their audacity, by which through scurrilous garrulity they insinuated themselves into the favour of many. Compare them to animals which seem to have come into existence to be ensnared and driven to their own ruin by their own instinct, as though induced by no allurements they of themselves hasten to throw themselves into the snares of Satan and of death; they are wild and rapacious, living on prey, and are often taken and destroyed while committing plunder, so that their own wickedness is the means of ensnaring and destroying them. On the thirteenth verse, connect the first words with what goes before and begin a fresh period, rendering it thus: counting riot in the day-time a pleasure, they are spots and stains, rioting in their own delusions, feasting together with you. The things said of them are meant to show that they were disgraceful and defiling; they rioted in carnal pleasure and in delusion, and associated with the faithful at their feasts. Say they place their happiness in their present enjoyments — we know that men excel brute animals in this, that they extend their thoughts much farther, so it is a base thing in man to be occupied only with present things, and our minds ought to be freed from the gratifications of the flesh unless we wish to be reduced to the state of beasts. Elsewhere, take the angels to be the good angels, who excel in strength, who are guardians of particular men and preside over provinces and kingdoms, and who are greater not than the devils nor than the false teachers, though both are true, but than dominions and dignities, than kings, princes and civil magistrates. And on the beasts, say these men are sunk below their own species, are like the horse and the mule without understanding, more stupid than the ox or the ass which know their owner and their crib, and being given up to a reprobate mind call good evil and evil good.

Call the verse about the angels a difficult one, and give the sense thus: the holy angels, represented as bringing an account of the actions of the fallen angels before the Lord in judgment, simply state the facts without exaggeration and without permitting anything of a bitter or railing spirit to enter into their accusations — compare the vision in Zechariah, to which the apostle evidently alludes. But these persons not only speak of actions they conceive to be wrong, but do it with untrue colourings and the greatest malevolence: the archangel treated a damned spirit with courtesy, saying only, The Lord rebuke thee, Satan, while these treat the rulers of God’s appointment with disrespect and calumny. Note that the words before the Lord are wanting in a number of manuscripts and most of the versions. Elsewhere say simply that the angels appear before the Lord to give an account of what they have seen and done on the earth. On the beasts, render them natural animals void of reason, following only the gross instinct of nature, governed neither by reason nor religion, intended to be taken with nets and gins and then destroyed because of their fierce and destructive nature — so these false teachers and insurgents must be treated, first incarcerated and then brought to judgment, that they may have the reward of their doings; and thus, by blaspheming what they do not understand, they at last perish in their own corruption, that is, their corrupt doctrines and vicious practices. But add the qualification that several such creatures seem born to be taken and destroyed only in the present disordered state of the world. On the day-time rioting, say that most sinners, in order to practise their abominable pleasures, seek the secrecy of the night, but that these bid defiance to all decorum, decency and shame, take the open day, and so proclaim their impurities to the sun — they glory in doing it in the face of the sun. Call them a disgrace to the Christian name, spots in themselves and blemishes to any church; say that sporting themselves means forming opinions which give licence to sin and then acting on them, and so rioting in their own deceits, making a jest of those whom they deceive and even jesting while they deceive their own souls. And on the last words, report that almost all the versions and several of the fathers, with two chief manuscripts, read in your love feasts rather than in their own deceivings, which is probably the true reading — from which it appears that they held a kind of communion with the Church and attended its sacred festivals, which they desecrated with their own unhallowed opinions and conduct.

debates: Which epistle, this or its parallel, was written first.
Whether the beings the angels decline to accuse are magistrates or evil spirits.
Whether the closing words read in their own deceivings or in your love-feasts.
Whether the rioting is by daylight or merely for the day.
Whether the word natural qualifies the beasts or the manner of their birth.
outliers: Ellicott argues the priority question from two consecutive verses and reaches opposite first impressions, then answers both in favour of this epistle.
Calvin states the objection to his own reading in full, names the rival reading, and refutes it from the parallel epistle.
Ellicott distinguishes beasts that cannot help rushing to ruin from men who seek it voluntarily and against nature.
Ellicott rejects riot as too strong and proposes a reading that turns the charge from shamelessness into living for the moment.
Barnes and Clarke reach opposite verdicts on the same variant, Barnes calling the received text certain and Clarke calling the other probable.
Clarke infers from his preferred reading that the false teachers were communicant members attending the love-feasts.
Wesley qualifies the claim that any creature was made to be destroyed by referring it to the present disordered state of the world.

14.pericope_label: Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin, beguiling unstable souls; an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children — which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness — but was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass, speaking with man’s voice, forbad the madness of the prophet

schools.summary: Read the first clause as eyes full of an adulteress, the word full denoting that the passion has wholly seized and occupied the mind, so that the eye sees nothing else but occasion for its indulgence; note that the eye is usually the first offender, the inlet to corrupt desire and the medium by which it is expressed, and that there is often much in dress, mien and gesture fitted to charm it. Render the next clause literally, that cannot be made to cease from sin, and find the reason in these men’s own principle: it was precisely because they refused to suffer in the flesh and on the contrary gave the flesh all possible licence that they could not cease from sin; note also that one pair of manuscripts reads a form that is probably only a misspelling. Take the participle for beguiling strictly as enticing with bait, note that the word occurs twice in this Epistle and only once elsewhere, and remark that the metaphor from fishing may point to a fisherman of Galilee. Take the heart exercised as a rhetorical metaphor from the gymnasium, the word being that used of training for the games; read in covetousness in the singular with the best manuscripts and versions; and render the last phrase children of malediction — they are devoted to execration, malediction having adopted them as its own, a Hebraism like son of perdition. On the name, say that Bosor seems a dialectal variation from Beor arising out of peculiar Aramaic pronunciation, and count it a slight indication that the writer was a Jew of Palestine; or offer the alternatives, that the name was corrupted, that the father may have had two names, or that Greek speakers changed it because it was more easily pronounced, noting that the Seventy read the ordinary form. Set out the resemblance to Balaam: that he was a professed servant of God, that he was governed by covetousness, and that he induced others to the same sin, having counselled the Moabites to entice Israel into licentiousness, as these men corrupted the church. Note that the past tenses of this verse are quite in harmony with the view that the chapter is a genuine prediction, a future foretold with such confidence being commonly spoken of as already past; and that a comparison with the letters to the seven churches gives countenance to including the Nicolaitans among the teachers stigmatised. On the last verse, render it literally, he had a conviction of his own transgression, and state the transgression precisely: knowing the blessedness of Israel, and having leave to go only on condition of blessing, he went still cherishing a hope of being able to curse and so win the promised reward. Render the beast a dumb beast of burden, noting that in Palestine the ass was the common one, horses being rare. Then correct forbad to hindered, and observe that the trivial discrepancy some would urge between this passage and the history disappears, since the objection is that not the ass but the angel forbad Balaam, whereas it was the ass which hindered his infatuation from hurrying him to his own destruction. Add that the word for madness is a very rare formation, the only known example of the form, probably coined by the writer and chosen for the sake of its sound beside the word for prophet.

Take the metaphor of the bait to remind the faithful to beware of hidden and deceitful arts, comparing their impostures to hooks that catch the unwary to their destruction; and note the reason for caution given in the word unstable, that is, when we have not struck firm roots in faith and in the fear of the Lord — from which it follows that they have no excuse who suffer themselves to be baited by such flatteries, since this must be ascribed to their own levity. Let there be a stability of faith, and we shall be safe from the artifices of the ungodly. On the exercised heart, note the word is of doubtful meaning, one editor rendering it rapines; prefer lusts, since having condemned incontinence in their eyes he now seems to refer to the vices latent in their hearts, and do not confine it to covetousness. On the last phrase, say they may be called execrable either actively or passively, that is, that they brought a curse with them wherever they went, or that they deserved a curse. Then say that as he has referred to the injury done by the example of a corrupt life, so he repeats that they spread by their teaching the deadly poison of impiety in order to destroy the simple; compare them to Balaam, who employed a venal tongue to curse God’s people, and to show that they are not worthy of a long refutation, say that Balaam was reproved by an ass and his madness thus condemned. Dwell on the judgment: it was a dreadful thing that the angel made himself known to the ass before he did to the prophet, so that the ass, perceiving God displeased, dared not advance farther but went back, while the prophet, under the blind impulse of his own avarice, pushed forward against the evident prohibition of the Lord — and what was afterwards answered to him, that he should proceed, was an evidence of God’s indignation rather than a permission. As the greatest indignity, the mouth of the ass was opened, that he who had been unwilling to submit to God’s authority might have that as his teacher; and by this miracle the Lord designed to show how monstrous a thing it is to change the truth into a lie. Ask then by what right Balaam had the name of a prophet, when he was addicted to many wicked superstitions, and answer that the gift of prophecy was so special that though he did not worship the true God he might yet be endued with it, and that God has sometimes caused prophecy to exist in the midst of idolatry, in order that men might have less excuse. And apply it: this warning is equally suitable to the present age, for it prevails everywhere that men use scurrilous raillery to deride God and the Saviour and ridicule all religion under the cloak of wit — these are worse than Balaam himself, because they pour forth their maledictions gratuitously, where he, induced by reward, attempted to curse. Elsewhere note that the seventh commandment is violated not only by unclean actions and obscene words but also by unchaste looks, and that this is how the Jewish teachers explain the precept; and that Balaam’s governing iniquity was covetousness, which led him into the rest.

Render the first clause as of an adulteress, the man being ever bent on gratification, so that an adulteress stands constantly before his eyes and they can take in no other object; and report the variant, that several manuscripts with the Coptic, Latin and Old Latin and several of the fathers read of adultery instead. On the next clause say the sense is which cease not from sin: they might cease, but they do not, for they love and practise it; and note that another variant would require the rendering, having eyes full of adultery and incessant sin, the images of sinful acts floating continually before a disordered and impure fancy, a figure of speech very common in the Greek writers. Take the beguiling from adulterers seducing unwary and trifling women, and the exercised heart from the competitors in the Grecian games who trained themselves in wrestling, boxing and running — these had their hearts schooled in nefarious practices. On Balaam, say he forsook the right way as one to whom God had shown it, preferring the reward Balak offered to the approbation of God, and that the way of Balaam is his counsel, that the Moabites should give their most beautiful young women to the Israelite youth to entice them into idolatry. On the name, say two ancient manuscripts and some versions have the ordinary form, and that the difference seems to have arisen from mistaking one Hebrew letter for another closely resembling it; or say more briefly that this is how the Chaldeans pronounced what the Jews called Beor. Note that Balaam loved, that is, earnestly desired, though he did not dare to take, the money Balak would have given him for cursing Israel. And on the dumb ass, ask whether the apostle is not referring to the speech of the ass as given in two of the Targums, where she says, Woe to thee, Balaam, thou sinner, thou madman, there is no wisdom found in thee — words containing nearly the same expressions as his.

debates: Whether the name Bosor is a textual corruption or a dialect form.
Whether the ass or the angel hindered Balaam.
Whether the exercised heart refers to covetousness or to lust more widely.
Whether cursed children means they bring a curse or deserve one.
How Balaam could be called a prophet at all.
outliers: Four commentators give four different accounts of one misspelt proper name.
Ellicott uses the dialect form of the name as evidence that the writer was a Palestinian Jew.
Ellicott notes the fishing metaphor twice in this letter and suggests it points to a fisherman of Galilee.
Ellicott removes an alleged discrepancy with Numbers by correcting forbad to hindered.
Clarke finds the ass in two Targums using almost the words of this verse, sinner and madman together.
Ellicott argues from the tense that the chapter is genuine prediction rather than description after the fact.
Calvin allows that the gift of prophecy could rest on a man who did not worship the true God.

17.pericope_label: These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest, to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever — for when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh those that were clean escaped from them who live in error — while they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption

schools.summary: Take the first figure of a spring or watering-place dried up in the desert, which entices and mocks the thirsty traveller and may lead him into danger by drawing him from where there is water; it was always a sad disappointment to come to a well expecting water and find it dry, and so these teachers only aggravate the trial of men seeking the refreshing influences of the gospel. Take the second of a cloud which promises rain as it rises, exciting the farmer’s expectation, and is then driven off by the wind — those who put on the appearance of virtue while destitute of all goodness being like a light cloud that makes a show of rain and afterwards vanishes. Note that the word for mists is an old word for fog, found here alone in the New Testament, and that the word for the squall that drives them is rare. Then weigh the argument for a Hebrew original: one Hebrew word occurring only twice in the Old Testament is rendered by the Seventy in the one place by the word here used for well and in the other by the word the parallel epistle uses for cloud, so that the same Hebrew might have produced wells without water here and clouds without water there. But coincidences of this kind may easily be mere accidents of language, and must be shown to be numerous before a solid argument can be based upon them; remember too that the writers in both cases were Jews writing in Greek while thinking probably in Hebrew, so that the same Hebrew thought might suggest a different Greek expression in the two cases. Note also that the parallel passage is much fuller than this one and reads more like an amplification of it than this like a condensation of that, since a simile so admirably suitable to false guides as wandering stars would hardly have been neglected. On the swelling words, say that truth is simple and delights in simple statements, expecting to make its way by its own intrinsic force, while error is noisy and declamatory and hopes to succeed by substituting sound for sense; and sum the phrase as exaggeration, unreality, boastfulness and emptiness, carrying on the idea of the waterless wells and the driven mists, great pretensions and no results. Then correct the next clause in two places: the adverb should be by a little, that is scarcely, not clean, and the verb should be present, not past — those who are scarcely escaping, that is, the unstable souls mentioned above. The word rendered scarcely occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, while the word our version read is frequent; hence the change, an unfamiliar word being by a slight alteration turned into a familiar one, the two Greek words being much alike. Note also that the preposition before the lusts of the flesh points to the sphere in which the enticement takes place, while the wantonness is the bait used to entice. On the liberty, take it as a specimen of the great swelling words, loud high-sounding talk about liberty, and cite what two fathers report of the doctrines of a famous heresiarch to show the kind of liberty such teachers promised, being freed from righteousness to become the slaves of sin. Give the ignominious word its full force, slaves of corruption, rather than servants; and hear in the last clause an echo of the saying that everyone who continues to commit sin is the slave of sin, words which this writer may himself have heard, and perhaps also of a passage in the epistle to the Romans, with which there is nothing improbable in his being well acquainted in his last years — the improbability would rather be in supposing that he did not know it.

Show by the two metaphors that they had nothing within though they made a great display: a fountain draws men to itself by its appearance, because it promises water, and clouds as soon as they appear give hope of immediate rain to irrigate the earth; so these excelled in boasting and displayed some acuteness of thought and elegance of words, but were dry and barren within, and the appearance of a fountain was fallacious. Say they were driven by the wind, either without rain or bursting into a calamitous storm, so that they brought nothing useful and were often very hurtful; and by naming the darkness allude to the clouds which obscure the air, as though for the momentary darkness they now spread there were prepared a much thicker darkness to continue for ever. On the swelling words, render the phrase overswellings of vanity, meaning what is pompous, inflated and bombastic, and empty and unprofitable with it; say they dazzled the eyes of the simple with high-flown stuff of words so that they might not perceive the deceit, for it was not easy to captivate their minds with such dotages unless they were first besotted by some artifice, and that this grandiloquence was very suitable for covering their shifts and trumperies. Name the ancient teacher who, with those like him, made words unheard of before, by the empty sound of which the unlearned were smitten and ensnared by their reveries, and say there are fanatics of a similar kind at this day. On the liberty, show their inconsistency, that they falsely promised liberty while they themselves served sin and were in the worst bondage, for no one can give what he has not. But answer the objection: it sometimes happens that wicked men wholly unacquainted with Christ preach usefully concerning his benefits, so observe that what is condemned here is vicious doctrine connected with impurity of life, the design being to obviate the deceptive allurements by which they ensnared the foolish. The name of liberty is sweet, and they abused it so that the hearer, loosed from the fear of the divine law, might abandon himself to unbridled licentiousness; but the liberty which Christ procured and offers daily by the gospel is altogether different, for he has exempted us from the yoke of the law so far as it subjects us to a curse, that he might also deliver us from the dominion of sin so far as it subjects us to its own lusts. Where lusts reign, therefore, and where the flesh rules, the liberty of Christ has no place whatever; and the godly are to desire no other liberty than that which leads those set free from sin to a willing obedience to righteousness. Elsewhere say these men looked like angels of light, transformed themselves as ministers of righteousness, had a form of godliness and boasted of their knowledge, promising great advantages to their followers, but were like deceitful brooks or dry wells, having nothing but the filth and slime of error, destitute both of the grace of God, which is comparable to water, and of the truth of heavenly doctrine, which is like the rain that fills the wells. And on the liberty they promised, say it was not Christian liberty, which lies in freedom from the dominion and guilt of sin, but a carnal liberty from the law of God as a rule of life, from the civil magistrate, from masters and from parents, and a liberty to neglect the ordinances of the gospel at pleasure.

Say the word of truth is the water of life, which refreshes the souls that receive it, but that deceivers spread and promote error and are therefore set forth as empty, because there is no truth in them; and that as clouds hinder the light of the sun, so do these darken counsel by words wherein there is no truth. Seeing that they increase darkness in this world, it is very just that the mist of darkness should be their portion in the next. Observe the irony of what follows: in the midst of their talk of liberty these men are the vilest slaves, their own lusts having gained a complete victory over them, so that they are actually in bondage. When men are entangled they are easily overcome; therefore Christians should keep close to the word of God and watch against all who seek to bewilder them.

Say that these are persons who by their profession should furnish the water of life to souls athirst for salvation, but have not this water — teachers without ability to instruct, sowers with no seed in their basket. Nothing is more cheering in the deserts of the east than to meet with a well of water, and nothing more distressing, when parched with thirst, than to meet with a well that contains none; and in a time of great drought, to see clouds beginning to cover the heavens raises the expectation of rain, but to see them carried off by a sudden tempest is a dreary disappointment. Note the various reading which puts mists or thick darkness in place of clouds, supported by the chief manuscripts, and observe that it is very different in sound but nearly the same in sense. Take the mist of darkness reserved for them as eternal separation from the presence of God, the utmost degrees of misery and despair, into which false and corrupt teachers will be sent, the most downcast vassals of perdition. On the swelling words, say the Greek signifies things of great magnitude, grand and sublime, but sometimes inflated and bombastic: these teachers spoke of great and high things and promised their disciples the greatest privileges, pretending themselves to a high degree of illumination, but all was false and vain, though it tickled the fancy and excited the desires of the flesh, which indeed appears to have been their object — whence some think the impure sect of the Nicolaitans is meant. And on the liberty, say it was either to live in the highest degrees of spiritual good, or freedom from the Roman yoke, or from the yoke of the law, or from what they might term needless restraints; their own conduct showed the falsity of their system, for they were slaves to every disgraceful lust. Explain the closing maxim from the ancient custom of selling for slaves those whom men had conquered in war, the law being that a man might either kill him whom he overcame in battle or keep him — so the person overcome by his lusts is the slave of those lusts. Say more briefly still that they promise freedom from needless restraints and scruples, while they are themselves slaves of corruption, even sin, the vilest of all bondage.

debates: Whether the victims had clean escaped or are scarcely escaping.
Whether the coincidence of wells here and clouds in the parallel points to a Hebrew original.
Whether the text reads clouds or mists driven by the tempest.
What liberty the false teachers were promising.
Whether a wicked teacher can preach profitably about Christ.
outliers: Ellicott corrects a verb and an adverb together and reverses who the victims are.
Ellicott explains the corruption by an unfamiliar Greek word being altered into a familiar one much like it.
Ellicott weighs the Hebrew-original argument and rejects it on method, not on the evidence.
Ellicott argues from the fuller parallel that the other epistle amplifies this rather than this condensing it.
