Calvin refuses to conclude from the verse that an ungodly man cannot preach usefully of Christ.
Barnes contrasts the simplicity of truth with the noise of error in a single sentence.
Ellicott suggests the writer had heard the saying he echoes, and knew the epistle to the Romans.

20.pericope_label: For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning — for it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness — but it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, the dog is turned to his own vomit again, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire

schools.summary: Guard the opening clause carefully: escaping the pollutions of the world does not necessarily mean that these had been true Christians and had fallen from grace, for men may outwardly reform and escape the open corruptions that prevail around them while having no true grace at heart; neither does the knowledge named imply that they were true Christians or ever had any saving knowledge of the Redeemer, since there is a knowledge of the doctrines and duties of religion which may lead sinners to abandon their outward vices and has no connection with saving grace. Or take the contrary line, that the knowledge is of the same mature and complete kind spoken of in the first chapter, showing that these men were well-instructed Christians; and note that the preposition means in knowledge rather than through it, pointing to that in which the escape consists. Explain the word for entangled from its root meaning of braiding or interweaving, so that they are implicated in these vices like an animal caught in a net; observe that apostates usually become worse than they were before their professed conversion, as a reformed drunkard returning to his cups becomes more abandoned than ever; and note that the last clause is almost an exact reproduction of a saying in the Gospels, and should be made to correspond with it. Say it were better for them because they would not then have dishonoured the cause of religion, nor sunk so deep in profligacy, nor incurred so aggravated a condemnation; and add that if men are resolved on being wicked they had better never pretend to be good, and that if they are to be cast off at last it had better not be as apostates from the cause of virtue and religion. On the two proverbs, note that the word rendered proverb is used elsewhere only in one Gospel, where allegory would render it best; that if the first comes from the Book of Proverbs we have here an independent translation of the Hebrew, since the Greek version gives an entirely different rendering with dog the only word common to the two; that the second is nowhere in the Old Testament, so that both may come from popular tradition rather than Scripture; that the word for vomit was possibly formed by the writer himself and the words for wallowing and for mire are rare; and that in the Greek neither proverb has a verb, as often in such sayings. Add that the second is probably from a Gentile source, since it concerns the habits of hogs, on which the heathen moralists also wrote. Then draw the doctrinal conclusion: under all the appearances of reformation their evil nature remained, as really as that of the dog or the swine, and that nature finally prevailed; the dog and the swine had never been anything else than dog and swine, and these persons had never been anything else than sinners, so that this passage would seem to demonstrate that there never had been any real change of heart and of course no falling away from true religion, and it should not be quoted to prove that true Christians may fall from grace and perish.

Show how pernicious the sect was that led men consecrated to God back again to their old filth, and exhibit the heinousness of the evil by comparison, for it was no common sin to depart from the holy doctrine of God. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness; for though there is no excuse for ignorance, the servant who knowingly and wilfully despises the commands of his lord deserves a twofold punishment. There was besides ingratitude, because they wilfully extinguished the light of God, rejected the favour conferred on them, and having shaken off the yoke became perversely wanton against God, and as far as they could profaned and abrogated the inviolable covenant of God which had been ratified by the blood of Christ — the more earnest, then, ought we to be to advance humbly and carefully in the course of our calling. By naming the pollutions he shows that we roll in filth and are wholly polluted until we renounce the world, and by the knowledge he means the gospel, whose design is to deliver us from the defilements of the world and lead us far away from them. Note next that the doctrine of a holy life, though common to all, is yet peculiarly taught to those whom God favours with the light of his gospel, and that they who make themselves slaves again to the pollutions of the world fall away from the gospel — but distinguish: the faithful also sin, yet as they allow not dominion to sin they do not fall away from the grace of God nor renounce the profession of sound doctrine they once embraced, for they are not to be deemed conquered while they strenuously resist the flesh and its lusts. Then, since the example disturbs many when men who had submitted to the obedience of Christ rush headlong into vices without shame, remove the offence by saying that this happens through their own fault, and because they are pigs and dogs; it hence follows that no part of the sin can be ascribed to the gospel. The gospel is a medicine which purges us by wholesome vomiting, but there are many dogs who swallow again what they have vomited, to their own ruin; and the gospel is also a laver which cleanses all our uncleanness, but there are many swine who immediately after washing roll themselves again in the mud. And remind the godly to take heed to themselves, unless they wish to be deemed dogs or swine. Elsewhere note that the phrase for the pollutions of the world is rabbinical, that ignorance is not good nor to be excused but would have been a lesser evil, and that the proverb quoted is true both in fact and in its application.

Explain the word for pollutions from its use for the noxious particles of effluvia proceeding from persons infected with contagious diseases, from dead and corrupt bodies, from stagnant and putrid waters and marshes, by which the sound and healthy may be infected and destroyed; and represent the world as one large putrid marsh or corrupt body, sending off its destructive vapours everywhere, so that none can escape its contagion and none be healed of the great epidemic disease of sin but by the mighty power of God. Improve the image with the saying that the whole world is one great diseased man lying extended from east to west and from north to south, and that to heal this great sick man the almighty Physician descended from heaven. Then say that if, after being healed and escaping the death to which we were exposed, we get entangled and enveloped with these again, the latter end will be worse than the beginning, forasmuch as we shall have sinned against more light. Say it had been better for them not to have known, because they have sinned against more mercy, are capable of more sin, and are liable to greater punishment; and note that the whole religion of Christ is contained in the one commandment to love God with all the heart and one’s neighbour as oneself, which by the grace of Christ is possible to every man. On the proverbs, trace the first to the Book of Proverbs, give the rabbinic parallel in which Orphah is returned to her mire while Ruth persevered in spirit, and the Greek saying that one should go and reason with the swine lest he be rolled in the mire; call it a true proverb, for a dog will eat up his own vomit and a swine, however carefully washed, will wallow in the mire again. Then apply it plainly: the poor sinner, having heard the gospel, was led to loathe and reject his sin, and on applying to God for mercy was washed from his unrighteousness; but he is here represented as taking up again what he had rejected and defiling himself in that from which he had been cleansed. Here is a sad proof of the possibility of falling from grace, and from very high degrees of it too — these had escaped the contagion that was in the world, they had had true repentance and cast up their sour-sweet morsel of sin, they had been washed from all their filthiness, and this must have been through the blood of the Lamb, yet after all they went back. Elsewhere say more briefly that such are all men in the sight of God before they receive his grace, and after they have made shipwreck of the faith.

debates: Whether the apostates here had ever been true Christians.
Whether the passage proves that the truly converted may fall from grace and perish.
Whether the two proverbs come from Scripture or from popular tradition.
Whether the men entangled again are the false teachers or their victims.
What the knowledge is by which they escaped the pollutions of the world.
outliers: Barnes argues from the proverbs that there was never a real change of heart, and forbids the verse to be used against perseverance.
Clarke argues from the same verse that falling from very high degrees of grace is possible, and that these had been washed by the blood of the Lamb.
Calvin takes neither side, laying the fault on the men themselves so that nothing can be charged against the gospel.
Ellicott holds the knowledge named proves these men were well-instructed Christians, against Barnes on the same words.
Ellicott finds the first proverb an independent translation of the Hebrew, since the Greek version renders it quite differently.
Robertson traces the second proverb to a Gentile source and cites a heathen moralist on the habits of hogs.
Clarke reads the word for pollutions as a medical term and makes the world one putrid marsh.
